Waist bender in the run game, still a bit of a project in that regard
athletic_notes: PFF grades — Receiving 78.3, Run-Blocking 81.3, Red-Zone 70.7, YPRR 1.77, Contested Catch 59.4%. Height 6-7, Weight 264, Arm 34.375, Hand 11.00, 40-yard 4.64, 20-shuttle 4.08, Bench 21, Vertical 31.0, Broad 10-2.
summary: At 6-7 and 270, huge athlete with top-10 run-blocking grade. May be more of a luxury piece than a necessity at tight end, but if you have a specific role for him, you wont find anyone better.

strengths: Electric after the catch for a tight end — 30 broken tackles on 111 catches last two years
Speed to legitimately threaten the seem, gets off the line quickly
Versatility to split to the slot or out wide — 65 snaps as outside receiver last year
weaknesses: Ball skills nowhere near as reliable as youd like from a tight end
Run routes like theyre drawn on paper too often, wont set up defenders with stem
Strength as an inline blocker is not what you might expect from an Iowa tight end
athletic_notes: PFF grades — Receiving 85.2, Run-Blocking 70.2, Red-Zone 53.1, YPRR 2.15, Contested Catch 37.5%. Height 6-3, Weight 245, Arm 31.125, Hand 10.25, 40-yard 4.59, 20-shuttle 4.25, Vertical 35.0, Broad 10-3, 3-cone 6.91.
summary: One of the best college tight ends weve graded in the PFF college era. LaPorta has the tools to be a difference-maker at the position.

strengths: Elite speed for the tight end position, broke 20 MPH at the Senior Bowl
Lab built frame with large hands, linebackers and safeties just sort of fall off him in coverage
Contact doesnt seem to phase him, able to get off press because of it
weaknesses: Really raw as a route runner, looks like hes counting steps to get to his breaks
Not shifty after the catch — two broken tackles over his entire career
Doesnt utilize lower half as a run blocker, will stop feet to engage
red_flags: Knee injury ended 2022 after two games
athletic_notes: PFF grades — Receiving 79.2, Run-Blocking 48.3, Red-Zone 54.3, YPRR 3.38, Contested Catch 33.3%. Height 6-6, Weight 253, Arm 32.625, Hand 10.375, 40-yard 4.61, Vertical 36.0, Broad 10-5.
summary: One of the best athletic projects in the draft class. Musgrave has the goods but not the refinement — can still contribute due to his tools while developing.

strengths: Moves like an athlete, very smooth in everything he does
Very natural runner, plus body control on full display in open field
Well proportioned tight end who utilizes size advantage, plays through contact with ease
weaknesses: Looked like a man amongst boys against low-level of competition, some aspects wont translate
Speed isnt going to scare linebackers, much more of an underneath threat
Drop issues will be worth monitoring — 7 drops in 2021 and a 10.8% drop rate in career
athletic_notes: PFF grades — Receiving 76.5, Run-Blocking 69.4, Red-Zone 63.2, YPRR 2.32. Height 6-5, Weight 254, Arm 32.75, Hand 10.00, 40-yard 4.69, 20-shuttle 4.29, Bench 23, Vertical 34.0, Broad 10-2, 3-cone 7.08.
summary: Very similar to Dallas Goedert, also a South Dakota State product. Kraft ticks all the boxes of a starting tight end in the NFL.

strengths: Great at finding space between zones, has field vision that a quarterback can trust
Ability to sink into his hitches and really stop on a dime
Swift off the line with enough speed to outrun slower linebackers
weaknesses: Little dynamism with the ball in his hands, lacks wiggle — two broken tackles his entire career
Doesnt use size to his advantage as route-runner and struggles to avoid contact
Will turn 25 years old early in his rookie season
red_flags: Will turn 25 early in rookie season
athletic_notes: PFF grades — Receiving 78.7, Run-Blocking 63.3, Red-Zone 55.7, YPRR 2.13, Contested Catch 28.6%. Height 6-5, Weight 251, Arm 32.875, 40-yard 4.63, 20-shuttle 4.27, Vertical 33.5, Broad 10-7.
summary: Wolverines secret weapon. High floor tight end who should be a Day 1 starter thanks to refinement as an inline blocker.

strengths: Natural athlete, really see him shine with the ball in his hands
Can go up and get it, looks comfortable playing the football in the air or hurdling after the catch
Hard-nosed football player, not going out of bounds and doesnt back down as a run-blocker
weaknesses: Barely featured in Penn State offense, hard to get a strong feel with only 38 targets all season
Often left looking around for who to block in run game
One of the few NFL players youll see whose wingspan is actually smaller than his height
athletic_notes: PFF grades — Receiving 73.1, Run-Blocking 60.5, Red-Zone 67.3, YPRR 1.44, Contested Catch 62.5%. Height 6-4, Weight 253, Arm 31.125, 40-yard 4.70, 20-shuttle 4.46, Bench 23, Vertical 36.0, Broad 10-4, 3-cone 7.25.
summary: Plus receiving tight end who you hope develops enough as a run-blocker. Look elsewhere if you want a run-blocker, but if TE is a receiver first in your offense, Strange is your man.

strengths: Absurd athlete, truly an all-time tester for the position
Massively long frame thats diced up, very low body fat for 255 pounds
Burst out of lateral breaks that can give big windows over the middle of the field
weaknesses: Too often the one getting bodied at the catch point
Still fairly trim frame, gets bullied as a run-blocker because of it
Only one full year of playing time, couldnt see the field in three years at Penn State
red_flags: Undisclosed injury cut 2022 short after five games
athletic_notes: PFF grades — Receiving 90.7, Run-Blocking 67.3, Red-Zone 67.5, YPRR 1.26, Contested Catch 33.3%. Height 6-7, Weight 255, Arm 34.0, Hand 10.25, 40-yard 4.55, 20-shuttle 4.12, Bench 23, Vertical 40.0, Broad 10-8, 3-cone 6.87.
summary: All-time combine performance — thats how youd put together a tight end in a lab. Tape shows he still needs a lot of work, though.

strengths: Outstanding straight line speed, a real seam threat
Smooth when rounding off posts or digs over the middle of the field
Flashes plus body control adjusting to off-target passes downfield
weaknesses: Unplayable as an inline blocker, lacks play strength — might as well be a wide receiver
Very unreliable hands especially by tight end standards — 11.2% career drop rate
Counts steps on hard route breaks, no explosiveness out of them
athletic_notes: PFF grades — Receiving 78.0, Run-Blocking 36.6, Red-Zone 51.8, YPRR 1.68, Contested Catch 38.5%. Height 6-5, Weight 239, Arm 32.25, 40-yard 4.54, Bench 20, Vertical 36.5, Broad 10-1.
summary: Too much of a tweener to feature at tight end or receiver unless he changes his body composition entirely.

strengths: Enough speed to get vertical and threaten seams of a defense
Easy adjustments outside of his frame, reliable hands
Outstanding at finding targets on the move, perfect fit for split zone-heavy scheme
weaknesses: Inconsistent precision in his breaks, can snap off breaks but not them sharp
Build up speed instead of suddenness, not going to split him wide because of it
Not sure if he has the requisite heft in his lower half to take on NFL defensive ends
athletic_notes: PFF grades — Receiving 68.5, Run-Blocking 69.5, Red-Zone 76.5, YPRR 1.11, Contested Catch 28.6%. Height 6-7, Weight 248, Arm 31.5, 40-yard 4.69, Vertical 33.5, Broad 9-7.
summary: Model of consistency with 300+ receiving yards in each of past three years. Worry at Whyles age that he may be capped out, but can be a reliable, if uninspiring, starter.

strengths: Rare blend of size, speed, and horsepower-type strength in the pocket
Elite arm talent on par with Josh Allen with more consistent placement
Impressive pocket manager with economical movement in tight confines
Strong feel for manipulating coverage in the middle of field and flats
Processes leverage well and protects receivers with pass placement
Stamina to maintain speed after breaking or avoiding multiple tackles
weaknesses: Inexperienced with only one year as a full-time college starter
Release footwork and drop pacing can slow adjustments to pressure
Sails some intermediate passes when stepping in the bucket
Lapses adjusting to pre-snap coverage looks
Waits one to two beats longer than necessary on some throws
red_flags: Torn meniscus in high school led to December 2021 knee surgery
Missed 2021 games with knee, head, and hamstring injuries
summary: Inexperienced and raw but rare conceptual and athletic traits for a passer. A unique amalgamation of Cam Newton, Daunte Culpepper, and Josh Allen with impressive learning ability and on-field decision-making for a one-year starter. Highest ceiling in the class if landing spot gives him time to develop.

strengths: Skilled pocket manager with well-developed drop-back and play-action game
Consistently delivers accuracy off back foot and off platform
Well-defined and efficient two-, three-, five-, and seven-step drops
Ability to self-scout and adjust placement decisions within the same game
Keeps eyes downfield while climbing and flushing the pocket
Layers throws over shallow coverage with pinpoint accuracy
weaknesses: Not a dynamic runner with limited stop-start or cutback ability
Targets can sail due to wide stance and slightly stiff front leg
Does not always account for ancillary zone defenders and their leverage
Can anticipate pressure too early and move outside the pocket prematurely
Overlooks timely deep shots as secondary reads
red_flags: Missed 2021 Akron game with shoulder injury
summary: The safest quarterback in this class with a well-developed pocket game and play-action foundation. Skilled pocket manager with the physical, technical, and conceptual tools to become a competent and productive NFL starter. If he develops confidence with specific coverage looks, he could mature into a top-producing starter.

strengths: Quintessential creator who finds solutions pre-snap and off-script
Holds safeties with his eyes on one-on-one vertical routes
Quick and compact arm motion with efficient weight transfer
Maneuvers tight pockets with blend of athletic ability and efficiency
Accounts for leverage of ancillary coverage to protect receivers
Patient with zone windows and can place ball back-shoulder when needed
weaknesses: Durability question from size at listed 204 pounds
Drop footwork lacks depth and variety for the pro game
Misses open receivers despite eyes downfield while maneuvering
Red-zone play has repeated moments of immaturity and risk
Pressure can force accelerated processing and unfavorable leverage throws
red_flags: Missed week and a half in 2022 with throwing shoulder injury on October 1
Body type and weight durability concerns for NFL physicality
summary: Young has a high enough ceiling to finish his career as the most productive option of this class as well as the earliest to make an impact. A Montana/Brees-style field general fused with Wilson/Murray creativity whose floor is lower due to size. If a team leverages his short and intermediate prowess while creating shot plays, he could emerge as a statistical force.

strengths: Excellent play fakes with variation of pacing on drops
Strong pocket management combining footwork, structure, and intuition
Executes hard counts and shoulder fakes to manipulate coverage
Clutch player with anticipation on in-breaking routes
Quick and compact release with smooth two-step drop
Quick processor against pressure and reads
weaknesses: Intermediate velocity shy of adequate against tight man coverage
Overestimates arm strength on boundary routes
Toe points to boundary rather than the breaking target on outs
Defenders over the top of receivers stress his decision-making
Must learn better 2nd-and-long down-distance management
red_flags: Missed five weeks with a high ankle sprain
Below-average arm strength may limit ceiling
summary: Haener is the Brock Purdy of this class—a skilled passer lacking elite athletic traits for an early draft pick, but could emerge as a journeyman starter if and when he earns playing time. His pocket feel, play fakes, and mobility fit well in an Andy Reid-style scheme. Likely to work his way from third QB to a backup role by 2025.

strengths: One of the best sets of drops in this class with precise timing
Underrated arm strength and guts of a burglar in the vertical game
Quick and confident processor of man-to-man coverage
Effective stop-start movement with good quickness as a runner
Maneuvers pockets with controlled incremental footwork
Pinpoint off-platform accuracy with various arm angles
weaknesses: Ball security lapses only tucks ball when pursuit draws near
Varieties of zone coverage slow his processor and lead to late throws
Late to deliver wide-open zone routes in intermediate and vertical ranges
Short and small for an NFL quarterback at 5-11 and 192 pounds
Red-zone lapse of judgment when failing to take quick opportunity
red_flags: January 2023 arrest in Dallas for public intoxication
Size concerns could push him to UDFA status
summary: A Cinderella Georgia walk-on turned two-time national champion with underrated NFL arm talent and creative off-script ability. Not as creative as Russell Wilson or Seneca Wallace but fits stylistically. Could develop into a capable backup and potential journeyman starter depending on how NFL teams weigh his size.

strengths: Physical tools and baseline accuracy to start in the NFL
Aggression and confidence to attack downfield
Efficient three-step, five-step, one-step, and two-step drops
Baits edge pressure and climbs only when defender is a step away
Efficient spin-and-roll escapes from unblocked edge pressure
Nimble enough to execute schemed throw-backs under pressure
weaknesses: Needs to refine drop and release footwork at slower speeds
Struggles reading leverage of man coverage on out-breaking routes
Does not throw the ball away nearly often enough
Makes questionable choices under pressure in red zone and own area
Ball carried low and loose from frame as a runner
red_flags: Fumbled in green zone against Slippery Rock late in the half
Small-school competition level concerns
summary: Bagent has the tools to develop into an NFL quarterback of note and is worth monitoring. Ideal developmental path would be intermittent playing time to refine mechanical and conceptual details. With time, he could acclimate to NFL speed and become a game manager who knows his limitations.

strengths: Most impressive vertical game in the class with strong range and placement
Patient passer who reads the field well and holds defenders with eyes
Strong spatial awareness as a runner with shifty lower-body movement
Acceleration to turn the corner on near-side perimeter runs
Works across width of field with multiple reads in timely fashion
weaknesses: Quick throws on screens and RPOs often less than pinpoint accurate
Wide baseball stance limits torque generation on short throws
Sails vertical throws when rushing release due to pressure perception
Bounces on balls of feet leading to unintended pocket drift
Lacks confidence in velocity on intermediate middle-of-field throws
red_flags: Foot surgery in late November 2021 after playing through broken bone
Childhood heart condition discovered during COVID-19 screening
summary: A former four-star recruit who led TCU to the National Championship Game with an impressive vertical game reminiscent of Jeff Blake. Duggan is a patient passer who reads the field well but must refine footwork and release stance. Could develop into a compelling backup with productive stints as a starter if minor flaws are sharpened.

strengths: Excellent drop game that rivals C.J. Stroud for best in class
Compact over-the-shoulder delivery with good trunk and hip rotation
Patient in the pocket and integrates feel with downfield vision
Good movement and feel for pressure when it arrives
Layers throws over linebackers with good anticipation on digs
Holds safeties to one side before working late to boundary
weaknesses: Must speed up timeline when backed up in own territory
Identifies leverage poorly on man coverage working opposite side
Pocket clock for anticipating pressure not quite sharp enough
Throws high when pressure compresses pocket without room to step
Pinpoint accuracy diminishes between 35 and 40 yards
red_flags: Missed 2021 Independence Bowl with lower-body injury
Missed October game from mid-September injury against Arizona State
Missed 2019 game with concussion in late October
summary: Hall has the skills to be a better NFL prospect than former BYU teammate Zach Wilson. An accurate passer on the cusp of developing greater across-the-board accuracy that could elevate him to starter grade. Should be in running for a No. 2 or No. 3 role as a rookie.

strengths: Defined two-step and three-step drops from shotgun and pistol
Sturdily built to maneuver tight confines with confidence
Good feel for the pocket and throws well on the move
Baits edge pressure within step before sidestepping or climbing
Spin-and-roll and reduced-shoulder escapes under interior pressure
Opens body during drops to manipulate screens and backside digs
weaknesses: Often identifies open targets but waits too long to pull trigger
Arm strength limits tier as an in-demand backup
Ball security lapses as a runner with ball hanging at waist
Must improve manipulation of middle-of-field defenders
Footwork after maneuvering pocket is suspect and difficult fix
red_flags: Hamstring and forearm injuries during career
summary: Tune reminds of Gardner Minshew with skill and confidence maneuvering the pocket but limitations with arm strength. Spread offensive background appeals to Air Raid teams. Could stick to a roster early in career and work into a No. 2 role within 1-3 seasons if confidence with identification-to-action improves.

strengths: Effective vertical passing game with easy quick-game recognition
Calm demeanor delivering ball with pressure arriving from edge or middle
Good placement on shallow routes breaking into middle of field
Manipulates linebackers with legs and pump fakes for space
Can deliver 55 yards from pitch point with pinpoint on vertical breaks
Better build-up speed than sudden acceleration for long-runway gains
weaknesses: Front leg lacks bend on release causing passes to sail
Consistently 1-2 beats late delivering vertical shots against man
Stiff-legged runner without much bend in knees and hips
Lacks confidence closing identification-to-action gap as a passer
Misses late pre-snap movement of blitzing safeties
red_flags: ACL tear against South Carolina in November 2022
Age 25 which may turn off teams preferring younger players
summary: A productive executor at Virginia Tech and Tennessee who can fit in NFL spread offenses and develop into a contributor. Has effective vertical passing paired with quick-game recognition and runs as scrambler or designed ballcarrier. Could become a first-tier backup 2-3 years down the line.

strengths: Quickness and mobility to develop into a playmaker inside and outside pocket
Good feel for throwing receivers open in middle of field
Sudden hand-eye coordination to pluck errant snaps and deliver on time
Varies throwing motion from over-the-top to three-quarter around pressure
Layers targets over shallow zone defenders on the move
Full complement of drops and play-action fakes from center
weaknesses: Release stance gets too wide with toes pointing in opposite directions
Anticipation against over-the-top coverage must improve
First inclination against interior pressure is retreat rather than climb
Reactive in a negative way when pockets are tight
Fails to account for ancillary coverage peeling off to cut off routes
red_flags: Built more like a receiver than a quarterback for pocket punishment
summary: Thompson-Robinson has similar strengths in the passing game to Lamar Jackson in the middle of the field and as a mobile playmaker. A smart player capable of growing into a savvy veteran who manages a team within physical limitations. Career reserve who could emerge as a reliable No. 2.

strengths: Aggressive passer who reads leverage well in intermediate game
Confidence to make tight-window throws from the pocket
Willing to fit targets into tight windows of shallow zones
Manipulates middle-of-field defenders by opening up during drops
Deep-over pinpoint accuracy at 31 yards with pressure bearing down
Identifies edge pressure and climbs 1-2 steps past it
weaknesses: Tips off intentions to defense and must develop disguise
Not enough anticipation on routes against tight or off-man coverage
Ball carried wide from frame and drifts low changing direction
Feet can get wider than shoulder width on three-step drop
Stares down receivers working vertical zones tipping off coverage
red_flags: Missed parts of November and December 2020 with foot surgery
Pair of fumbles from uncertain read fakes vs. Michigan
summary: A former walk-on who has been an effective Big Ten quarterback with confidence to make tight-window throws. Might be better served earning playing time elsewhere to refine game management. Has the aggression and confidence to become a viable backup in the NFL.

strengths: Big, strong-armed, and quick physical prototype for the position
Arm strong enough to make every requisite NFL throw
Competent set of drops with efficient seven-step from center
Quick spin that works against edge defenders off read plays
Strong enough to work through glancing hits from smaller defenders
Vertical accuracy with pinpoint back-shoulder at 35 yards opposite hash
weaknesses: Footwork not where expected for a player with NFL offensive coach
Waits for additional visual confirmation forcing rushed throws
Leads receivers into hits that disrupt plays and drives
Misses quick and identifiable opportunities to throw receivers open
Drifts into pressure when he initially had right idea to set and throw
Rushes drops and setups compared to 2021 performances
red_flags: Entire game consistently inconsistent from phase to phase
Lacks strong coverage and game-management IQ
summary: Levis has the physical tools to become a franchise quarterback but significant technical, conceptual, and game-management flaws. The difference between Levis and Josh Allen is that Allen had sound throwing mechanics and pocket movement. Not projecting early-round optimism for him to rework fundamentals quickly enough.

strengths: Prototypical size and arm talent at 6-6 and 231 pounds
Strong arm with ability to layer targets over middle of the field
Fits well in a play-action system with seam routes off fakes
Pinpoint accuracy on short middle and intermediate middle throws
weaknesses: Internal clock for pressure in the pocket needs to be faster
Missing opportunities for easy check-downs that prolong drives
Stunted pocket manager development due to poor Stanford pass protection
summary: McKee is a physically impressive prospect with a strong arm but the lack of quality pass protection at Stanford may have limited and stunted his development. A second-string quarterback with playable short-term skills and the physical profile of a starter.

strengths: Rare explosion, body mobility, and strength of a top bell-cow back
Versatile stiff-arm that works between tackles and in open space
Presses within two steps of lead blocks to set up cutbacks or bounces
Excellent one-cut burst downhill with notable first step
Can high-point targets with quick accurate hands
Curvilinear movement to bend around safeties in open field
weaknesses: Can get impatient pressing creases in short-yardage and red-zone
Eschews easy gains for cutbacks or bounces requiring elite footwork
Pass protection has work ahead for NFL contribution level
Tries to live up to expectation of breakaway play on every run
Leaves yards on the field by not attacking tight creases
red_flags: Missed two games with dislocated elbow in 2020
summary: Inexperience and tight lower body limit burst but contact balance and vision are elite. A compelling 1.01 dynasty target with potential for Tomlinson-like elite production through interior running, breakaway plays, passing game, and red-zone work. Should make an instant and significant impact as a lead back in an era with gap-run revival.

strengths: Dynamic mover with light, sudden, and efficient footwork
Slippery runner with underrated contact balance in traffic
Excels at flipping hips to change direction in tight spaces
One of the two most elusive backs in the open field in this class
Acceleration to beat play-side linebackers to near or far boundary
Understands when to reduce shoulder to avoid linebacker reaches on wheels
weaknesses: Confidence issues pressing 1-2 steps more for bigger gains
Tries cutback too early leaving designed gains on field
Overextends and drops head on double-team and stand-up blocks
Lacks explosive chip on box defenders to release cleanly into routes
Leaves feet unnecessarily when tracking targets lacks confidence
red_flags: Undisclosed lower leg injury late November vs. Duke, missed Pitt game
Played 7 of 10 games as a freshman missing 3 due to injury
summary: Slippery, dynamic mover in the spectrum of Marshall Faulk, Charlie Garner, and Kevin Faulk. A safe 1.02 in this era of football who should land with an offense that gives him touches by air and gap play. Upside of 1,300-1,500 scrimmage yards and 10-15 touchdowns as peak expectation.

strengths: Shifty, creative back with slippery power and compact running style
Low pad level from beginning to end of a run aids power and balance
Elite spatial awareness in the open field
Excellent curvilinear movement to bend sharply at high speed
Strong stiff-arm with good reach and location against backside pursuit
Accelerates well from cuts and outruns safeties through the second level
weaknesses: Leans too hard on juke moves in the open field
Long plants to set up lateral cuts minimize quick-feet value
Stop-start movement minimizes yardage when defense has man advantage
Long sticks and stutter steps slow him enough for backside pursuit
summary: A Jamaal Charles-spectrum back with explosive athletic ability, dynamic movement between tackles, and slippery power. Talents belong in the same tier as Robinson and Gibbs. Understanding of how to set up runs and elite footwork potentially make him a compelling lead option rather than just a change-of-pace.

strengths: Gets skinny between the tackles and hits tight creases decisively
Sense of urgency with hitting the hole fast with body adjustments
Excellent lateral quickness to juke edge defenders with jump cuts
Curvilinear movement to bend around pursuit in tight quarters
Accelerates well after contact and beats safeties up the flat
Strong stiff-arm to ward off reaches from linebackers in tight quarters
weaknesses: Claps onto the ball when it arrives at the numbers on underhand catches
Lapses with hands when turning up the field before securing ball
Ball security elbow can be tighter moving laterally in space
Can drop head towards pursuit as lead blocker missing angles
Gets tossed aside by larger linebackers when sustaining laterally
red_flags: Toe injury vs Texas Tech in 2021, shut down after Thanksgiving
Concussion in 2022 against Alabama
Hamstring injury cost him an NFL Combine workout
summary: Excellent selection of footwork and moves to set up pursuit with vision and decision-making that is the best in this class. A top-five running back talent whose injury risks could deflate value 1-2 rounds. If NFL selects him in rounds 2-4, a strong indication there are no significant off-field issues worth betting first or second round in dynasty.

strengths: Patient zone runner inside and outside the tackle box
Tackle-breaker with good contact balance across multiple levels
Decisive gap runner who times his pace behind lead blockers
Efficient stutter jukes to press unblocked defenders into blockers
Drags defenders wrapped high for 3-5 yards on multiple attempts
Stiff-arm is one of the assets of his game especially on perimeter
weaknesses: Claps onto the ball with mixed hands position on catches
Pad level often too high in goal-line situations
Drops head towards pursuit as lead blocker missing angles
Gets tossed aside quickly by larger linebackers laterally
Speed is good but more quick than fast in open field
red_flags: Minor meniscus scope surgery before freshman year at Michigan
Battled multiple injuries in 2019
summary: A rugged Arian Foster starter kit with potential to play heavier and maximize his power. Has become a patient zone runner with tackle-breaking contact balance and starter-grade ability despite committee-tier hands. Could become a workhorse if he refines passing-down skills and adds 5-10 pounds.

strengths: Smooth running back with power and vision plus notable acceleration
Effective inside zone runner who reads linebackers and safeties
Hip mobility to flip hips and bend away from tight pursuit
Effective stiff-arm combined with spin move to work free of reaches
Sneaky-good acceleration gets on top of secondary pursuit fast
Good hand-eye coordination with fewer pass-catching technique flaws
weaknesses: Pad level inconsistent between the tackles on slower-developing concepts
Leans heavily on spin move in open field
Overextends on stand-up pass-pro strikes without uppercut hip roll
Allows targets into frame arriving on numbers in wide-open areas
Ball carriage high but loose at elbow outside heavy traffic
red_flags: Knee injury in first half vs Michigan, missed National Title Game
Rib injury missed 2021 season finale
Missed November 2021 Baylor game with foot injury
summary: Like Lamar Miller, a smooth back with power and vision who does everything well enough to be a starter with potential to be more. Appears more explosive than Charbonnet with a lower center of gravity and more promise on passing downs. Capable of top-12 production for multiple seasons.

strengths: Well-built back with a low center of gravity and excellent footwork
Burst and power to finish plays with impressive speed for weight
Patient to allow pulling blocks to develop on gap plays
Curvilinear movement and speed to bend on near-side flat runs
Effective jump cuts, sticks, and short-area quickness
Works through multiple reaches, wraps, and hits on single runs
weaknesses: Loses matchups as pass protector when overextending aggressively
Tips hand with cutback too soon on zone plays with double-teams
Abandons technically-sound punch to deliver harder hit
Prone to carrying ball under right arm even on plays designed left
Can miss small interior creases that do not require full bounce
red_flags: Three fumbles in 2022 drop Depth of Talent Score 1-3 points
Ankle injury in 2021 and multiple spring injuries
summary: One of the better-kept secrets of this promising running back class with a low center of gravity like Ray Rice. Could make an instant impact in a gap-heavy offense, but ball security and pass-pro overextension are concerns. Could become a lead back in a gap-heavy scheme or a career reserve depending on whether he hangs onto the ball.

strengths: Explosive enough to flip the field with decisive moves through creases
Acceleration to bend away from safeties with angles over the top
Breaks multiple tackles in open field with effective stiff-arm
Effective with chipping defensive ends and linebackers off play-action
Careful hugging backside blocks to avoid unblocked backside defenders
Overhand technique above head for high targets without leaving feet
weaknesses: Lacks sudden re-acceleration when forced to stop-start
Consistently step late reading penetration into the backfield
Lapses reading puller leverage or cuts back a step too soon
Lacks a punch and box defenders can mow through his protection
Drops head before cut-block shoot missing what he is hitting
Prone to keeping ball under right arm bending runs up left boundary
red_flags: Concussion in 2021 cleared a week later
Missed 2021 Syracuse game for undisclosed reason
summary: Reminds of Damien Harris based on build with a versatile enough skill set to produce as a starter in a power running game. Lacks athletic ability to hold a lead role over multiple seasons but explosive enough to flip the field. Could begin his career as a low-volume role-player and become a reliable co-starter.

strengths: Smart runner with excellent short-area quickness and receiving skills
Decisive into creases as a gap runner using speed and pacing
Skilled with trap and counter using pace to set up blocks
Developed a punch rolling through his hips as a pass protector
Route-running skills against man and off-man coverage
Pressing within a step of blockers on zone plays
weaknesses: Lacks the acceleration of a starter despite quickness
Allows targets into frame when placed on his numbers
Reacts towards open space rather than setting up leverage
Needs quicker reach to edge pressure after play-fakes
Lack of size, power, and long speed demands compensatory factors
summary: Gray is a smart runner with short-area quickness and receiving skills but lacks starter acceleration. More likely to become a valuable passing-down back in a reserve role with stretches as a committee back. Needs a strong offense around him to deliver statistically meaningful starter production.

strengths: Explosive player with strength capable of identifying and setting up creases
Reads leverage on off-tackle zone and finds appropriate cutbacks
Hits gap plays decisively, accelerating in timely fashion
Acceleration to beat linebackers downhill off guard or far-side edge
Good reach with stiff-arm to ward off safeties coming downhill
Adjusts stride length to set up creases or avoid backfield penetration
weaknesses: Turns back or runs backward at fast-arriving unblocked pursuit
Veers toward engaged blockers rather than staying in open lane
Claps onto ball with underhand position at chest height
Long hip-opening step causes stumbling on bounces

summary: Bradley possesses a nice arm with clean mechanics. He made a few pretty deep passes over the past two years, mostly outside the numbers. His fundamentals allow him to maximize his arm talent, which is average for the NFL level. His athleticism allows him to scramble and pick up first downs. He also is not afraid to step up in the pocket. His game starts to fall off when he is asked to throw with touch on short or intermediate throws; his mechanics break down and he looks uncomfortable. He also tends to lock onto his primary read. Bradley's smaller hands also impact ball security and ball placement. BOTTOM LINE: Bradley is an intriguing prospect with a decent arm, an encouraging play style and good mechanics. How quickly he can learn to read NFL defenses and how much he can improve on touch throws is his key to locking down a preferred backup spot.

summary: Coleman originally committed to Michigan State as a twosport athlete, and he transferred to Florida State in 2023. He is an impressive 6foot-4 and 215-pound athlete who enjoys getting physical with cornerbacks, as he constantly catches passes through contact. While that yields jaw-dropping feats of strength, his lack of separation ability is concerning for the next level — there just aren't a lot of guys who make a living as consistent contested-catch receivers. The ones that do are often some of the best receivers in the league. BOTTOM LINE: Coleman is a top-tier athlete for the position from an explosiveness standpoint. summary: Harrison is one of the most complete prospects you will find. He displays an understanding of how to win at the position like few college players do. summary: Worthy has difference-making NFL speed. He got off to a hot start at Texas, owning about every freshman receiving record in the Longhorns' record book. He's not just a straight-line sprinter — his footwork, acceleration, one-cut burst and vertical speed must be accounted for on every play. However, his play strength is a concern, as he does not fight off contact well and can get locked up against press coverage. BOTTOM LINE: Worthy must be identified pre-snap in all situations due to how easily he can take a pass to the house if not accounted for. If he can get stronger and learn to be a better hand fighter with defenders, he can be an impact pass catcher as a WR2/3.

summary: All is an all-around tight end prospect. He is a willing move blocker who is often detached from the line of scrimmage to lead, get to the second level or perform split-zone blocking responsibilities. He brings blocking fundamentals and good hand usage, though he could display more of a finisher's mentality. He understands how to use leverage and angles to wall off defenders without holding. He has big hands, although he did have frustrating drops in college. All is a better athlete than he gets credit for, as his change-ofdirection fluidity yielded high separation rates in 2023. He also showcases good balance for yards after the catch. BOTTOM LINE: All could use a bit more nastiness in his game, but this is a player with a versatile, contributing skill set who projects as a TE2 at the next level if he can stay healthy.

summary: Barner has been a late bloomer throughout his football career, culminating in a career year in 2023. In 2022, he was slow off the line of scrimmage and in his routes. This past season showed a quicker, more explosive version of himself, though one that is still below average for the NFL. His calling card is blocking. His best work comes from an inline or wingback position, where he can push people around. He takes pride in his blocking, as he's constantly looking for work and has excellent grip and core strength to maintain blocks. He can erase secondary players near the line of scrimmage, and he can even push defensive ends around, at times. BOTTOM LINE: Though Barner won't give you much in the receiving game, he is an ideal TE2/3 for a team that likes to run heavy formations.

summary: Bell is a "tweener" for the tight end position but brings versatility as an offensive weapon with experience at inline tight end, wingback, running back and wide receiver. He has solid overall athleticism, with top speed and balance being his best traits. While his routes are good for a tight end, they are still rounded and don't create much separation against single coverage. He is also still finding a feel for zone coverage, too often simply running his route instead of speeding up or slowing down for space. Bell brings nice pop at contact as a blocker but does not maintain blocks consistently. BOTTOM LINE: Bell is an easy roster depth piece because of how many roles he can play, but he needs to find a better feel for zone coverage as a receiver and must maintain blocks better.

summary: Bowers is one of the most well-rounded tight end prospects to ever enter the NFL. At Georgia, he was the SEC's Freshman of the Year. In both his sophomore and junior seasons, he was an All-American and the John Mackey Award winner (nation's top tight end). His build-up speed is good for the NFL, which is why he has elite after-the-catch ability. He has some of the strongest hands you'll see for a tight end. As a blocker, he might be the strongest pound-for-pound tight end you'll find. His versatility allows him to be an elite pre-snap movement piece, as defenses have to account for where he is at all times and in all formations. BOTTOM LINE: Outside of being on the smaller side, Bowers is a dream tight end prospect who can be an impact player in the slot, out wide and inline. Add in his reliable blocking ability on the line and in space, and you have an ultimate chess piece offensive weapon with All-Pro potential.

summary: Holker will be one of the older prospects in the class. He started his football career at BYU and transferred to Colorado State in 2023. Though smaller for the position, listed at 6foot-4 and 235 pounds, he is a well-rounded athlete. He has a good first step and decent build-up speed to be a consistent vertical threat, especially over the middle. He displays strong hands for making contested catches over the middle. He isn't a twitched-up athlete, so his routes are very rounded, which affects his separation potential. While he is a patient and fundamentally sound blocker, his lack of weight shows up against bigger front-seven players. BOTTOM LINE: Holker is a well-rounded, versatile tight end who can be a good depth piece to pay in multi-tight end offenses, but he likely lacks the top-tier athleticism to be a TE1.

summary: Johnson brings plus size to the tight end position, ranking above the 70th percentile in height and weight. His long arms are an advantage when he is blocking edge rushers and hauling in passes. He has decent build-up and long speed when getting vertical up the seam, but he lacks the difference-making change-of-direction ability, which limits his route tree. He makes his money from an inline spot as a versatile blocker and pass catcher in heavier formations. He is a strong blocker when he targets defenders between the shoulders, but he can sometimes get crossed up (another area where his limited lateral ability shows). BOTTOM LINE: Johnson brings alluring size to the position with plus length for blocking and when hauling in passes. He is a developmental tight end who shows runs good vertical routes and thrives when blocking, but he needs to be more consistent in both areas.

BOTTOM LINE: Reiman is a throwback tight end with size and physicality. He is limited as a lateral athlete but has the potential to be a TE2 in an NFL offense that likes bigger tight ends.

summary: Sanders, a former five-star recruit, looks like a super-sized athlete. Coming mostly from an inline or wing-back position, he is a constant vertical threat and a mismatch for most linebackers in coverage. His hands are reliable, as he did not drop a single pass in 2023. His explosive movement skills allow him to run routes like a receiver. If he wasn't on a team that also included Adonai Mitchell, Xavier Worthy and Jordan Whittington, he could've easily been a 1,000-yard receiver. He possesses all the tools to be an impact blocker, as well. His tape does include snaps where he lacks the necessary blocking physicality against smaller players. BOTTOM LINE: Sanders is a Tier 1 athlete for the tight end position. He is still mastering the nuances of tight end play, and he needs more of a mean streak consistently as a blocker. However, even with those concerns, what he brings to the table as a vertical threat is worth a top-50 pick.

He is tough at the catch point but has shorter arms, which hinders his catching ability. His catch rate could also be higher. summary: Stover flip-flopped between linebacker and tight end at Ohio State, so it's clear he is a versatile athlete. He has a great build with good body control and balance, which shows up particularly when blocking. He is an intelligent blocker with patience and strength for his size. In the receiving game, he has reliable strong hands for contested catches. He shows good burst out of his stance, but his long speed will not be a major difference-maker at the next level. His intelligence allows him to run a diverse route tree, but his lack of lateral flexibility and explosiveness limits his separation ability beyond vertical routes. BOTTOM LINE: Stover is a well-rounded, well-versed football player whose natural athletic ability and fundamentally sound approach to the position should make him a high-floor role player with TE1 potential.

summary: Wiley really was not used in the passing offense until this past year but showed that his best could be ahead of him. Being a tight end at the NFL level can be more demanding than people realize. You have to have a rare blend of size and movement skills that most humans don't have. Wiley has that combination. He maximizes his catch radius and has an extremely low drop rate. His route tree is limited by the number of routes he ran, but he has the natural athleticism to be a decent route runner. He needs to improve both his finishing mentality and footwork in blocking for better consistency. BOTTOM LINE: Wiley has an ideal size/athleticism combination to be a contributing TE2/3 at the next level.

summary: Pratt is a developmental prospect with good fundamentals, a clean release, quality fakes, and acceptable size and arm strength.
